name: Pore strips

lead: Pore strips are adhesive strips pressed onto damp skin, usually the nose, and peeled off to pull out the surface of blackheads. The nose looks cleaner right away and pores look less visible.

Blackheads are open comedones, follicles plugged with keratin and sebum whose dark colour comes from oxidation rather than dirt. The adhesive bonds to the plug and lifts it as the strip is removed, and Wikipedia says the strips can lift blackheads across an area. The plug returns as the follicle refills, so the effect is temporary, and published research on the strips is limited.

paras: Users wet the skin, press the strip on, wait until it dries and peel it off, typically once a week or so. They are sold over the counter and are often used alongside cleansers or exfoliating acids.
Wikipedia says pore strips can damage skin by tearing away surrounding skin and leaving pores wide open. No other safety data were found.

angle.text: Pore strips lift the surface of blackhead plugs off the nose, leaving a visibly cleaner surface straight away. The effect is temporary because follicles refill, and there is little clinical research on them.

lead: Pore strips are adhesive strips, usually applied to the nose, that are left to dry and peeled off to lift the visible surface of blackheads and sebum plugs. People use them for a quick, visible smoothing of the nose and cheek area: after a strip is removed, the dark dots of open comedones are often visibly reduced, so skin can look cleaner and clearer for a short time.[1]

A blackhead is an open comedo, a hair follicle plugged with keratin and sebum. Its dark colour comes from oxidation of pigment on exposure to air rather than from dirt or poor hygiene.[1] Wikipedia lists commercial pore-cleansing strips as one over-the-counter way to remove blackheads across an area, alongside the cyanoacrylate method dermatologists use, and notes that strips can leave pores wide open and tear away surrounding skin.[1]

Published research on pore strips as a blackhead treatment is limited. In the literature they appear mainly as a sampling tool: a 2018 study in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology compared surface swabs, pore strips and cyanoacrylate glue for sampling the follicular microbiome in 20 volunteers.[2]
infobox: Open comedones (blackheads), usually on the nose

paras: Pore strips are typically moistened onto the skin, left to dry and peeled off. The plug lifted is the surface portion of the comedo; the follicle below can refill with keratin and sebum.[1]

Comedones form when keratin and sebum block a follicle. Androgens increase sebum production, which is one reason comedones are common in adolescents. A comedo open to the air is a blackhead; one closed by skin is a whitehead.[1] Sebaceous filaments, which are different structures, are distinguished from comedones in the same source.[1]

Wikipedia reports that strips remove blackheads across an area but can damage skin by leaving pores wide open and tearing surrounding skin.[1] It lists other approaches: non-oily cleansers and mild soap, extraction by dermatologists or in salons after steaming, and retinoids and azelaic acid, which it says have some research support. It notes that squeezing can raise the risk of infection and scarring.[1]

In a 2018 study, pore strips were one of three methods (with surface swabs and cyanoacrylate glue) used to collect skin microbiome samples from the cheeks of 20 volunteers, with implications for acne research.[2] A 2026 review of the skin mycobiome in acne discusses sampling and fungal involvement in acne pathophysiology.[3]

No studies found testing pore strips as an acne or blackhead treatment. A 2018 study in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology used pore strips as a sampling method for the follicular microbiome.[2]
Pore strips are mentioned in body-care and skin-routine discussions as a quick, temporary blackhead remover.
